newsitem.title: USA: Clinton crows, Dole shows strength in tighter race.
newsitem.headline: Clinton crows, Dole shows strength in tighter race.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's political team crowed on Tuesday over hopes for a sweep of Northeast and West Coast states, while Bob Dole weathered a New Jersey storm as the presidential race tightened.

The latest Reuters tracking poll showed Dole just 5.3 percentage points behind Clinton, the Republican challenger's best showing since the poll began in August. The poll includes responses after Sunday's televised presidential debate.
Still, Clinton was confident enough to take the day off from campaigning after a Northeast barnstorming trip that included Connecticut, New Hampshire and Maine.
As Clinton stayed out of public view, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, "We increasingly see the possibility of a clean sweep in the Northeast."
McCurry added that the Dole campaign's purchases of television advertising in California, Oregon and Washington state suggest he is conceding those states, where Clinton enjoys substantial leads.
The Dole campaign in California sharply disagreed.
"They've been pitching that tall tale for four months now and it's as untrue now as when they first said it," said a Dole spokesman in California, Dale Neugebauer.
"We're running a very competitive campaign here," he said. "We're on the ground all over the state. It's a very aggressive effort. Clinton has a very tough record to defend out here."
Dole took his campaign on the road for the second day, rolling through the hotly contested state of New Jersey on a tour bus dubbed "Asphalt One," stressing his trustworthiness.

"I can give you example after example of Clinton saying one thing and then did another," Dole told a crowd of supporters. "When Bob Dole gives you his word you can go to the bank with it, he won't change his mind."
Perhaps Dole's most memorable line came in response to a boisterous backer in Lyndhurst, New Jersey, who shouted, "Please get Bozo out of the White House."
"Bozo's on his way out," was Dole's reply. The White House was unamused, with McCurry suggesting that Dole might have been "desperate" to have made such a riposte.
Heavy rain forced Dole to cancel two outdoor rallies and a fundraiser, leaving him to make impromptu stops at a diner and a church social hall in New Jersey before returning to Washington.

Nationally, the Reuters poll showed Clinton at 43.8 percent, Dole at 38.5 percent for a gap of just 5.3 percentage points. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was at 4.5 percent, 1.9 percent supported other candidates and 11.3 percent were undecided.

The poll was a rolling three-day average of results from about 300 interviews a day, Saturday through Monday. The Reuters/Zogby poll of approximately 900 likely voters had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
Daily tracking polls can show sharp fluctuations due to the relatively small sample of voters polled each day. Their value lies in tracking trends over a period of several days.
By contrast, a CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll released on Tuesday showed Clinton with 56 percent, Dole at 34 percent and Perot at 5 percent, with a 4 point error margin.

Common Cause, a campaign watchdog group, said on Tuesday it will ask the Justice Department to take action against both Clinton's and Dole's campaigns for what it called "potential massive violations" of campaign law. Details were to be announced on Wednesday.
